title: When a button feels slow: trace the wait
summary: A slow action can mean missing feedback, unnecessary waiting, a component that is not ready, or stale data undoing progress. Identify which stage is waiting before deciding what to optimize.
triggers: A button appears to do nothing after a click.
The server has finished, but the interface still shows the old action.
A panel opens, but its controls are not usable yet.
A successful action briefly reverts to its previous state.
Starting or attaching a terminal feels slow.
invariant:
- When a click seems ignored, report pending state before waiting for asynchronous work.
- When a result arrives but stays hidden, remove only the waits that are unnecessary for presenting that result.
- When an opened view is not yet usable, tie controls to its actual readiness signal.
- When progress reverts, check whether older reads can overwrite newer state.

The interaction must acknowledge the click, present confirmed progress promptly, and enable input only when it can work.
symptom: In MuxMap, attaching a terminal initially gave little indication of progress. After progress feedback was added, starting a session still waited for a full workspace reload before opening the panel. Creating a session, loading the panel, connecting the socket, and accepting input were separate milestones hidden behind one action.
cause:
The patches reveal an unnecessary dependency: the successful session response already contained the data needed to open the terminal, but the UI awaited `loadWorkspace()` first. A separate readiness signal controlled safe terminal input. An older workspace poll could also arrive after the new session.

For a similar slow button, trace the stages before changing code. These are recommended diagnostic checks, not a claim that timings were measured in this incident:

| What you observe | What to inspect | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No visible response to the click | State changes before the first await | Feedback may be missing even while work is happening. |
| The request finished, but the result is hidden | Work awaited after the response | An unrelated refresh may delay presentation. |
| The result is visible, but input is unusable | UI loading, connection state, application readiness | Visible, connected, and usable are different states. |
| The UI updates and then reverts | Older in-flight reads and state writers | A stale response may undo the action. |
| The main request itself is slow | Request timing and server work | Profile that stage; a spinner will not speed it up. |
solution:
1. Set request progress immediately and show loading or connection state for the stage actually in progress. Clear pending state and expose errors on failure.
2. Use the returned session directly to update local state and open its panel. Replace the session object so stale runtime flags do not survive a merge.
3. Enable terminal input only after the backend running status and the terminal write callback permit activation.
4. Increment a workspace revision when attaching a session. Discard workspace responses that began before that revision, so they cannot restore the old stopped state.
verification: Hold the session response: progress should appear immediately. Release it while holding the workspace refresh: the panel should open anyway. Hold the backend readiness signal: input should stay disabled. Release readiness and confirm a command reaches the terminal. Deliver an older stopped-session snapshot: it must not undo the new session. Repeat with API and connection failures. These checks are the acceptance criteria; the source does not establish a numeric speedup.
limitations: The same reasoning can help with opening an editor, launching a job, or generating a preview; these are possible applications, not other incidents recorded here. Keep waits that enforce authorization, consistency, or a real prerequisite. A backend running status is useful only if it is sent after setup. A client revision guard does not solve consistency between unrelated server writers.

commits.note: Added attach progress, lazy loading feedback, explicit connection readiness, and input gating.
Opened terminals from the returned session immediately and rejected older workspace responses with a revision guard.

attempts:
The first patch, `ccf900a`, added request progress, loading feedback, and explicit connection readiness. It still awaited the workspace reload after session creation. That improved feedback without removing the extra wait. The later patch, `69c72df`, removed that dependency.

The earlier input path also relied on an open socket, which did not prove that the terminal was ready to accept input. The readiness patch added an explicit gate. The evidence does not provide measured before/after latency.
